extracted.intended_audience: scientists, naturalists, philosophers of science, and educated readers debating evolutionary theory
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and methodological standards for critiquing or defending hypotheses about evolution, the origin of life, and the role of mind/teleology in natural processes. Emphasises empirical evidence, conceptual clarity, and thinkability of explanatory claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid argument from ignorance
rubrics_metrics.description: The fact that we do not know distinctly how an alleged transition has taken place, is transformed into the assumption that no transition has taken place.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not convert present ignorance or gaps in mechanistic detail into proof that a transition is impossible or supernatural. Example given: using unknown mechanism between non-living and living to infer a supernatural commencement of life is illegitimate (analogy to Kepler's hypothetical guiding-spirits).

rubrics_metrics.name: Express scientific doctrines in purely physical terms
rubrics_metrics.description: Under its rigorously-scientific form, the doctrine is expressible in purely-physical terms, which neither imply competition nor imply better and worse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When possible, recast explanations mechanistically rather than teleologically. Phrases like 'competition' and 'better/worse' may be convenient metaphors but are not essential to a rigorously scientific formulation; avoid implying a directing Will when a physical description suffices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use 'survival of the fittest' with its intended meaning
rubrics_metrics.description: The law is the survival of the fittest — i.e. the survival of those constitutionally fittest to thrive under the conditions in which they are placed — not simply the 'survival of the better' or the stronger.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be careful substituting colloquial words ('better') for technical ones ('fittest'); doing so alters the argument and can invalidate objections. Examples: parasitism and retrograde metamorphosis show that 'inferiority' by ordinary standards can be adaptive and advantageous in given conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be cautious with terminology (semantic fit)
rubrics_metrics.description: Words historically associated with teleology (e.g., 'evolution' as 'to unfold from within') can mislead when the scientific process they name does not embody the older sense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acknowledge and explain semantic differences; explicitly repudiate meanings not intended in the scientific hypothesis. The text notes explicit cautions have been issued about misreading 'evolution' in its older teleological sense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Require thinkability/conceivability of explanatory propositions
rubrics_metrics.description: A thinkable proposition is one of which the two terms can be brought together in consciousness in the relation said to exist between them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid accepting as 'understanding' any proposition that cannot be conceived coherently (called a 'pseudo-idea'). Example: treating 'Evolution is caused by Mind' as an explanatory, thinkable statement fails because the two terms cannot be coherently united in the required causal relation when one attempts to imagine how a series of states of consciousness could produce the infinitely-multiplied physical processes of the universe.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not posit Mind-as-cause without coherent mechanism
rubrics_metrics.description: The proposition that an 'originating Mind' is the cause of Evolution can be entertained only so long as no attempt is made to unite its two terms in thought; accepted as faith, not as an understanding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If one invokes a universal or ubiquitous Mind as causal, one must answer how a series of states of consciousness can causally account for the multitudinous simultaneous physical processes across the universe. If no intelligible account exists, the claim is metaphysical faith rather than scientific explanation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use progressive empirical evidence to bridge theoretical gaps
rubrics_metrics.description: Scientific discovery is day by day narrowing the chasm supposed to be impassable between the living and the not-living; examples include artificial synthesis of organic compounds and spectrum-analysis indicating element complexity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer and marshal empirical results that reduce apparent discontinuities (e.g., synthesis of organic compounds, spectrum-analysis showing 'elements' are complex, isomeric changes in colloids resembling life-like motion) instead of invoking unexplained forces or special causes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognise continuity/gradation rather than sharp chasms
rubrics_metrics.description: There is not a break or chasm between life which shows no mind and life which shows mind; development proceeds by infinitesimal gradations (illustrated by egg → chick → adult and human infant → adult).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use ontogenetic and phylogenetic continuity as evidence against claims of absolute discontinuity (e.g., between life and mind, or between plants and animals). The absence of sudden steps argues for gradualistic explanations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid rigid binary classifications when boundary cases exist
rubrics_metrics.description: Attempts to frame definitions that include all plants and exclude all animals (and vice versa) have repeatedly failed; lower types show community of nature (e.g., zoospores, locomotive diatoms, chlorophyll in some animals).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When definitions fail at lower/higher boundaries, reconsider the classification scheme rather than using the failure to argue for an ontological chasm. Consider intermediate sub-kingdoms cautiously and critically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analyse and preserve the technical sense of key terms
rubrics_metrics.description: Substituting terms (e.g., 'better' for 'fittest') or failing to note the technical sense of words changes arguments and can lead to invalid objections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly check that terminological substitutions do not alter the theoretical claim; explain why a chosen term was used. The author defends his choice of 'fittest' because it covers cases that 'better' would not.
